newsitem.title: USA: Waning rate hike hopes leave dlr down at US close.
newsitem.headline: Waning rate hike hopes leave dlr down at US close.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 16 - The dollar closed weaker against most major currencies, pressured by fading hopes for a near term increase in U.S. interest rates, currency experts said.
The Federal Reserve meets September 24 to decide whether to boost rates in order to keep inflation in check. Yet data released last week indicated price pressures were subdued.

"Of course, one of the reasons why the dollar had rallied ... is because of expectations the Fed would hike in September," said Brian McCarthy, market analyst at Ruesch International. "Those expectations are no longer as entrenched as they used to be."
The dollar finished at 1.5104/11 marks, down modestly from 1.5112/22 at the open. The U.S. currency also fell to 110.16/23 yen from 110.46/53.
While fewer may believe U.S. interest rates are headed higher this month, some economists still cling to the view the Federal Reserve will probably push up rates later this year.

"If it looked like we weren't going to have a rate hike this year, then the dollar would probably back off more," said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch. "But currently of Fed watchers who were being surveyed, around 60 percent of them expect a rate hike in November."

A strong rally in U.S. stocks and bonds last Friday had lifted the dollar at the end of the week. Stocks also shot higher on Monday. Although the dollar failed to gain, the equity market still lent the currency a measure of psychological support.
After soaring to 5905.47 earlier in the day, the Dow industrials ended nearly 51 points higher at about 5889, its second consecutive record closing high.
"It's really the stock and bond markets and their strength that's supporting the dollar at this point," said Ruesch International's McCarthy.

However, McCarthy warned, "If the stocks and bonds stop their rally or if they undergo a little bit of profit taking, that could be the excuse that the interbank traders are looking for to take profits on the dollar as well, based on their diminished confidence in the likelihood of a rate cut this month."
Dollar losses on Monday came as foreign exchange trading in Japan was closed because of the Respect for the Aged holiday and amid a lack of market moving American economic data.
Therefore, some analyst played down the dollar's declines.

"Really the market is just trading technically," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics. "There is no real incentive in the market today and people are trying to find a bit of a base."

In other trade, the dollar closed at 1.2405/15 Swiss francs, down from 1.2420/30 at the open. Sterling rose to $1.5567/77 from $1.5510/20, while the greenback inched higher to Canadian $1.3703/08 from C$1.3698/03.
